definitions.meaning: The wearing away of rock by moving water and wind, which loosen bits of rock and carry them away.
A steep face of hard rock by the sea, battered by waves at its base.
Moving water in the sea that rushes at the cliff and batters it, loosening bits of rock.
Water flowing along in one direction; it carries loose bits of rock away along the coast.
Moving air that wears at exposed rock and helps carry small worn-off bits away.
The hard solid material cliffs are made of; it does not crumble on its own and must be worn by a mover.

mechanismSteps: A hard cliff stands by the sea - the hard rock just stands there while waves rush at it all day.
The waves loosen bits of rock - wave after wave batters and cracks the cliff until a loose bit breaks off.
Moving water and wind do the wearing - the current and the wind carry the loosened bits away, so the cliff gets smaller.
objectives: Explain what erosion means: rock worn away and carried away by moving water and wind
Name the movers at the coast: waves, currents and wind, and say what each one does
Explain why rocks do not crumble on their own
subject: geography
title: Erosion: wind and water wear rock away

trap.explanation: The slip: Solid rock looks permanent, so the wearing seems to happen by itself rather than through moving water or wind. The fix: Rocks do not crumble on their own: moving water and wind do the wearing, loosening and carrying the bits away. Always look for the mover: waves loosen, currents carry, and wind wears.
trap.misconception: Rocks crumble on their own, with nothing doing the wearing.

workedExample: Trace one piece of rock from cliff to pebble. Step 1: the cliff stands by the sea and waves batter its base again and again. Step 2: the waves loosen a chip of rock and the chip breaks off and falls. Step 3: the current carries the chip away along the coast while the wind wears at the cliff and the chip, rounding the chip into a pebble. At every step a mover - waves, current or wind - did the work.
